Trump names intelligence chief Jay Clayton as new White House AI czar

Clayton had said AI was a ‘gamechanger’ but also posed ‘a threat’ during his confirmation hearing

Donald Trump on Sunday named Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence , to also serve as the new White House AI czar.

Clayton, who leads the US’s 18 intelligence agencies , previously served as the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan and led the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term.

During his Senate confirmation hearing , Clayton said AI was a “gamechanger” but it also posed “a threat”.

“When something’s both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it,” Clayton told lawmakers when asked about AI.

CBS News was the first to report that Clayton would be appointed White House AI czar.

In a social media post on Sunday, Trump announced that Clayton would lead what the US president called “the Super Intelligence Force (SIF)”.

Trump’s post also said the SIF would “coordinate the federal government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers, and super intelligence companies”.

Among those reacting on Sunday to Trump’s invoking the term “super intelligence” was SpaceX chief Elon Musk . Musk said on his social media platform X that SI was “better” than AI – and that he was renaming his aerospace company’s AI unit from SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI.

Senator Mark Warner, a Virginia Democrat who is vice-chair of the Senate select committee on intelligence, cautiously welcomed the appointment of Clayton, while noting that “the administration has resisted meaningful safeguards without offering a serious alternative for addressing the national security risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems”.

“I look forward to working with Director Clayton on ensuring the United States stays ahead of China and other adversaries, strengthening the security and resilience of our most advanced AI systems, and establishing rigorous testing and safeguards so that increasingly powerful systems remain secure, reliable, and under human control,” Warner added.

In September, Trump announced he was creating an “AI Force” and a czar to oversee the technology’s growth and monitor for “bad” development. The announcement came after tech industry leaders warned that AI was developing too rapidly to control and that it could harm humans.

The president has largely brushed aside concerns about AI development and the construction of datacenters, which power the technology.

Trump has insisted continued development is paramount to defeating China in the global AI race.

But to address concerns, the president created an advisory committee in addition to the czar – whom he previously promised would be led by a “high IQ” individual. Trump also recently met with AI industry leaders to discuss concerns.

On Tuesday, Trump and six executives signed an AI accord at the White House, promising to create internal and external monitors to ensure the technology is used as intended and any safety issues are addressed.

Trump had initially created the AI and cryptocurrency czar position when he returned to the White House in January 2025.

David Sacks, the venture capitalist and tech businessman, served as the administration’s AI and cryptocurrency czar until March 2026, when he reached his employment limit under his designation as a “special government employee”.

UK households should keep small supplies of cash, bottled water and tinned food at home in case of emergency or war, the Defence Secretary has warned.

Wes Streeting said Britain faces a growing threat of being disrupted by fires, floods, and enemy attacks, including cyber warfare.

He called for a "whole society approach" to strengthen national resilience, though he insisted people should remain "alert not alarmed" regarding potential risks.

Speaking to The Sun ahead of the Labour Party conference , he said: "It’s just a simple ask of people.

"Do they have what they need indoors, should they lose access to their online banking for a period? Should they have a power cut?”

open image in gallery

British households are being advised to stock up on tinned food. ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

It comes as the government releases a list of supplies for an emergency kit they say everyone should keep at home.

Here we look at the key items you should stock up on in case disaster strikes.

What should people stockpile?

Wes Streeting has advised the British public there are certain items they should store for emergencies.

He said: "These are basic things, and of course, you know, a lot of people just have that in their cupboard naturally.

"It’s having some cash at home, having a supply of bottled water indoors, having some tinned goods that you can access if your electric goes and you’re not able to cook on the hob or in the microwave.”

Nutritionists and “preppers” on social media also say people should consider intake of carbohydrates and protein, and so suggest items such as oats, rice and pasta be included in any stockpile.

Kidney beans, peanut butter and tinned fish provide high levels of protein.

open image in gallery

The government has asked people to stock up on tinned food and bottled water. ( Getty/iStock )

What should I keep in my emergency kit?

The government says people should put together an emergency kit that includes key provisions you and your household would need during a short-term incident lasting several days, such as a power failure or a disruption to your water supply.

Recommended emergency kit supplies include:

A battery or wind-up torch – torches are safer than candles.

A portable power bank for charging your mobile phone.

A battery or wind-up radio to get updates during a power cut – a car radio can be used, however in severe weather it might be safer to stay inside.

Spare batteries for torches and radio and a backup battery for any medical equipment you rely on.

A first aid kit (or some first aid items) including items such as waterproof plasters, bandages, a thermometer, antiseptic, eyewash solution, sterile dressings and gloves, medical tape for dressings, and tweezers.

Hand sanitiser and wet wipes for hygiene purposes when the water is off.

Polls close in first round of Brazil’s high-stakes presidential election

Leftwing incumbent Lula trying to fight off close rival Flávio Bolsonaro, far-right son of jailed ex-president

The polls have closed in the first round of Brazil’s highly polarised and high-stakes presidential election that could change not only the direction of Latin America’s largest country but that of the entire region.

The election pits the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, against the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of Donald Trump and the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup after his failed 2022 re-election attempt.

Late on Sunday Bolsonaro was leading Lula in partial results. With results in from almost 65% of the country, Bolsonaro had 49.8% to Lula’s 42.25%, while several other candidates stood in the single digits.

Lula and Bolsonaro have alternated as frontrunners in the final stretch, making the outcome unpredictable. In recent days both have focused on persuading undecided voters in hopes of reaching 50% plus one vote; if neither does, there will be a runoff on 25 October.

Brazil is one of the few Latin American countries that still has a leftwing government after a wave of rightwing and far-right electoral victories across the region and the US takeover of Venezuela after the capture of Nicolás Maduro.

The 80-year-old Lula has positioned himself as one of the last regional leaders still willing to say no to Trump, and has recently accused the US president of trying to interfere in Brazil’s election in Bolsonaro’s favour .

View image in fullscreen
Lula embraces a child as he leaves a polling station in São Bernardo do Campo after casting his vote on Sunday. Photograph: Alexandre Meneghini/Reuters
Like his father, who was Brazil’s president during Trump’s first term, Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, frequently praises the US president and has pledged to join the US-led anti-drug-cartel coalition that has killed dozens of people in airstrikes and carried out military operations across the region.

Voting on Sunday morning in São Bernardo do Campo, the industrial city where his political career began nearly half a century ago, Lula said: “People will have to choose between strengthening democracy and barbarism.” The incumbent played down polls released on Saturday that showed the race was wide open – they suggested either candidate could finish ahead and force a runoff, or even win outright on Sunday. “The poll that matters will be carried out today,” he said.

View image in fullscreen
Flávio Bolsonaro with his wife, Fernanda, after voting in Rio de Janeiro. Photograph: Silvia Izquierdo/AP
Flávio Bolsonaro, who voted in Rio de Janeiro’s north zone, urged supporters of other rightwing candidates to switch to him in a “protest vote”. “Our internal polls show people who would have voted for other candidates, who are also against Lula, already voting for Flávio Bolsonaro … I hope it’s enough to give us victory in the first round,” he said.
